items: Bridge = one veth traversal + iptables NAT per packet.
Measurable at high packet rates, invisible for web services.
Host mode removes both — benchmark before paying in isolation.
macvlan skips NAT but needs LAN cooperation and blocks the host.

a_bullets: VXLAN adds roughly 50 bytes of header per packet.
That lowers the effective MTU for the payload.

items: On Linux volumes and bind mounts both hit the host FS — equal.
The writable layer is the slow one, because of copy-on-write.
On Desktop, bind mounts cross a VM boundary (virtiofs/FUSE).

items: Databases on `--internal` nets with no published ports.
Let a reverse proxy be the only container holding host ports.
Isolation is only as good as the process privileges.
Secrets: tmpfs or a manager — never loose files or env vars.

blocks.title: inspect Leaks
blocks.text: Env vars are visible to anyone who can run `docker inspect` — that includes your secrets.

items: Volumes: portable and safe, but opaque — hard to browse.
Bind mounts: transparent, but glue the container to a host layout.
Isolate by default, open one hole at a time.
Know which of the three mount types you have before debugging.
Always a user-defined bridge: free DNS and real isolation.
`-p host:container`, host first. `EXPOSE` publishes nothing.
`localhost` inside is that container — bind services to 0.0.0.0.
Reach the host via `host.docker.internal` (+host-gateway on Linux).
Empty volume seeds from the image once — content and ownership.
A stale volume silently keeps yesterday's data.
Permissions are numeric: `--user`, `USER`, `chown`, `:Z`.
Container root is host root on a bind mount.

blocks.title: Debug Order
blocks.text: inspect, then 0.0.0.0?, then same network?, then firewall/MTU, then netshoot inside the target namespace.

blocks.title: Final Model
blocks.text: The image is the code, the network is the wiring, the volume is the state. Keep the three separate and containers stay disposable.

caption.text: Part 2 of DOCKER NETWORKING & VOLUMES. Your container can't be reached and your database just vanished — same root cause: namespaces gave it a private network and a disposable filesystem. This handbook walks the whole path: veth pairs and bridges, what `-p` really writes into iptables, embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11, volumes vs bind mounts vs tmpfs, and the numeric UID traps that only break after you deploy. Ten pages of study notes — save it before the next Permission denied.
